strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: jointly reconstructing appearance, geometry, and open-vocabulary semantics from unposed images in one feed-forward model, while accommodating both sparse and dense inputs.

The combination of VGGT initialization, novel-view photometric supervision, instance-guided semantic learning, and separate geometry/semantic sparsification is practically motivated. The instance-anchor contrastive formulation also reduces the stated complexity from pixel-pair quadratic cost to O(N_p K).

Results on ScanNet are strong: FLEG substantially outperforms the reported feed-forward baselines across 2, 8, 16, and 32 views, and its performance remains relatively stable as the number of views increases.

The reported inference times of 1.89–3.20 seconds compare favorably with the minutes required by per-scene language-field optimization. The qualitative results support the quantitative improvements in rendering and language-based localization.
The paper is generally well organized, clearly illustrates the overall pipeline, and appropriately attributes the principal pretrained models and source datasets.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is too narrow for the broad claims of reconstruction from “any views” and practical generalization. The principal comparison is only on ScanNet indoor scenes; there is no evaluation on outdoor or substantially out-of-distribution data, no camera-pose or geometric reconstruction metrics, and no quantitative evaluation of the advertised 3D editing capability.

Potential evaluation leakage cannot be assessed. InstanceMV-14K explicitly incorporates ScanNet and ScanNet++, while those same datasets are used for evaluation, but the manuscript does not specify scene-level training/validation/test splits or confirm that evaluation scenes were excluded from training and pseudo-label construction.

The baseline study is incomplete and partly confounded. Several cited feed-forward semantic Gaussian methods are not evaluated, and no strong general-purpose feed-forward reconstruction baseline such as AnySplat is included for novel-view synthesis. Fixed-view baselines are extended with an insufficiently specified post-processing procedure, making fairness difficult to judge.

Tables 1 and 2 report different FLEG mIoU/mAcc values for what appear to be the same ScanNet 16-view and 32-view settings, without explaining different subsets or protocols. This undermines confidence in the comparisons. Timing results also omit hardware, memory, preprocessing, and whether all baselines include equivalent stages.

The ablations do not isolate several claimed contributions: novel-view selection, feature aggregation, InstanceMV-14K and its scale, isotropic covariance construction, or different semantic voxel sizes. The sparsification evidence reports only Gaussian counts, not memory, latency, rendering cost, or accuracy-efficiency curves.

Important method details are missing, including voxel sizes, feature dimensionality, coverage threshold, contrastive temperature, photometric-loss coefficient, batch size, training duration, hardware, dataset sampling, and mask-generation/filtering procedures. There is also an apparent technical contradiction: the paper says semantic Gaussians use a smaller voxel size than geometry Gaussians while claiming this produces fewer, sparser semantic Gaussians; normally a larger voxel size is required.

The term “3D-annotation-free” is overstated without qualification: supervision is distilled from VGGT, whose geometric capability originates from prior 3D training, and part of InstanceMV-14K uses masks projected from 3D annotations. The method avoids direct 3D labels during its own training, but does not remove dependence on 3D-supervised priors.

As an Algorithms/General submission, the work is promising and shows large gains, but the missing split documentation, inconsistent reported values, limited evaluation breadth, and insufficient ablation/reproducibility information leave the central scientific case slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: efficiently constructing language-embedded 3D Gaussian representations from variable numbers of unposed and uncalibrated images.

FLEG is an ambitious integration of VGGT-based geometry, novel-view photometric supervision, instance-aware semantic distillation, and separate geometry/semantic sparsification. Supporting 2 to 32 input views with one feed-forward model is practically attractive.

The reported ScanNet results are strong: FLEG substantially outperforms the selected feed-forward baselines across reconstruction and semantic metrics, while the reported 1.89–3.20 second runtime compares favorably with per-scene optimization.
The proposed InstanceMV-14K collection is potentially valuable in scale, reportedly containing over 15 million images from approximately 14,000 scenes.
The manuscript is generally readable, and the overview and qualitative figures communicate the intended pipeline effectively.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared. I assess this primarily as Applied/Systems rather than Algorithms/General because its value lies mainly in integrating pretrained VGGT, CLIP, SAM2, Gaussian prediction, and sparsification at scale. This reduces the importance of limited component-level novelty, but it makes rigorous evaluation, efficiency accounting, data documentation, and reproducibility especially important; the paper is inadequate on those dimensions.

The evaluation has a serious potential train/test contamination problem. InstanceMV-14K explicitly incorporates ScanNet and ScanNet++, while the experiments and ablations evaluate on those same datasets. The manuscript does not specify scene-disjoint splits, deduplication, or safeguards against sampling evaluation frames or scenes during training. This omission prevents confident interpretation of the large gains.

Baseline fairness is not established. FLEG is a roughly 1B-parameter model initialized from VGGT and trained on a claimed 15 million images, whereas model size, pretraining, training data, and compute are not matched or even reported for the baselines. Fixed-view competitors are extended to many views using an unspecified DUSt3R-style post-processing procedure that performs increasingly poorly, making the principal 'any views' comparison particularly difficult to interpret.

The experimental scope is narrow relative to the claims. Results are confined to two closely related indoor scan datasets, with the main comparison only on ScanNet and ablations only on ScanNet++. There is no evaluation on held-out Internet video, outdoor scenes, object-centric data, cross-dataset generalization, camera-pose accuracy, geometric reconstruction, or robustness to irregular view coverage. The evidence therefore does not support reconstruction from arbitrary multi-view images or broad real-world applicability.

Important evaluation details are missing: numbers and identities of train/test scenes, target-view sampling, class vocabularies and text prompts, open-vocabulary segmentation protocol, image resolution at evaluation, hardware, memory consumption, and whether all timing measurements include feature rendering and semantic querying. Variance or repeated-run uncertainty is also absent.

The ablation study is much too limited for a multi-component system. It does not isolate novel-view selection, 3D feature aggregation, InstanceMV-14K or its individual sources, variable-view training, isotropic semantic Gaussians, voxel sizes, or confidence-weighted aggregation. It also lacks comparisons with simpler semantic pooling and sparsification alternatives. Consequently, the paper does not establish which proposed elements cause the reported gains.

The claimed efficiency of hierarchical sparsification is supported only by semantic embedding counts (6.4M to 2.6M), not end-to-end memory, latency, rendering speed, or accuracy-efficiency curves. The description also appears internally inconsistent: semantic Gaussians are supposed to be sparser, yet Section 3.4 states that they use a 'smaller voxel size' than geometry Gaussians, which would normally create more rather than fewer voxels. Equation 12 additionally refers to an undefined covariance symbol, making the implementation ambiguous.

The '3D-annotation-free' framing is overstated. Training depends on pseudo-3D point maps and camera poses from pretrained VGGT, and the ScanNet/ScanNet++ instance masks are described as being obtained by back-projecting their 3D annotations. The approach may avoid direct ground-truth 3D loss annotations, but it still consumes strong learned 3D priors and, for part of the dataset, information derived from 3D labels.

The new dataset is insufficiently documented for reproducibility and responsible reuse. There are no collection and filtering details, scene/source counts, mask-quality assessment, train/validation splits, licensing or redistribution discussion, or treatment of privacy and copyrighted Internet video. There is also no commitment or concrete plan for releasing the dataset, training code, or model weights.

Several claims outrun the evidence. The paper advertises accurate geometry, real-time downstream use, and 3D editing, but reports no geometry metric or downstream task, provides no editing method or quantitative editing evaluation, and shows only a small editing illustration. Overall, the promising system and strong reported table values are outweighed by unresolved leakage, comparison, documentation, and validation concerns.

strengths: The paper presents a practically valuable Algorithms/General contribution: a unified feed-forward system that reconstructs language-embedded 3D Gaussians from unposed and uncalibrated inputs ranging from 2 to 32 views.

The combination of novel-view photometric supervision, instance-guided contrastive learning, and separate geometry/semantic sparsification is technically coherent and addresses meaningful bottlenecks in semantic 3D reconstruction.

Results on ScanNet are strong and consistent. FLEG substantially outperforms feed-forward baselines in semantic segmentation and novel-view synthesis across all tested view counts, while remaining stable as the number of inputs increases.

The comparison with per-scene methods demonstrates an important efficiency advantage: reported reconstruction takes 1.89–3.20 seconds instead of approximately 10–20 minutes, while also producing better semantic scores.
InstanceMV-14K is potentially valuable: its approximately 14,000 scenes and 15 million images allow semantic training at a scale difficult to obtain with conventional 3D annotations.

The ablations support the importance of geometric distillation and instance-level supervision, while showing that sparsification reduces the semantic representation from 6.4M to 2.6M Gaussians with a small accuracy improvement rather than an evident quality penalty.
The manuscript is generally clear, well motivated, and visually effective; the architecture and qualitative results communicate the main idea well.
weaknesses: The evaluation is narrower than the broad 'any views' and practical-deployment claims suggest. Quantitative evidence is confined to indoor ScanNet/ScanNet++ data, with no evaluation on outdoor scenes, Internet videos, cross-dataset generalization, or substantially different camera trajectories.

Dataset and split documentation is insufficient. Because InstanceMV-14K incorporates ScanNet and ScanNet++, which are also used for evaluation, the paper should explicitly establish scene-level disjointness and report sampling, SAM2 prompting/tracking, filtering, mask-quality control, licensing, and intended release details.

Several relevant recent feed-forward methods discussed in the related-work section—such as SemanticSplat, SpatialSplat, UniForward, and GSemSplat—are not evaluated. Moreover, fixed-view baselines are extended through DUSt3R-style post-processing, so their sharp degradation with additional views may partly reflect an unfavorable adaptation rather than an intrinsic comparison.

The '3D-annotation-free' description needs qualification: supervision comes from a VGGT teacher carrying learned 3D priors, and masks for part of the training corpus are obtained by projecting existing 3D annotations. The approach avoids directly requiring 3D labels for every training sample, but is not independent of 3D supervision.

The sparsification exposition appears internally inconsistent: the semantic representation is said to be sparser, yet Section 3.4 describes using a smaller semantic voxel size, which would ordinarily create more rather than fewer occupied voxels. Exact voxel sizes and the direction of this relationship should be clarified.

Efficiency evidence is incomplete for a central claim. The model has roughly 1B parameters, but the paper omits training cost, inference hardware, peak memory, FLOPs, and semantic rendering/query speed. Gaussian count alone does not fully substantiate reduced memory and computation, and a multi-second reconstruction time should not itself be described as real-time without defining the downstream setting.

Claims of accurate geometry, recovered camera parameters, and 3D editing receive little direct validation: there are no depth, point-cloud, pose, or editing metrics, and editing is shown only briefly. Per-scene comparisons also omit novel-view synthesis quality.

The ablations are limited and do not independently test the proposed multi-view feature aggregation, novel-view selection policy, isotropic semantic covariance, voxel sizes, or performance/quality trade-offs. No limitations or failure-case analysis is provided.

strengths: Evaluated as an Algorithms/General contribution, the manuscript presents a useful unified system for pose-free, feed-forward reconstruction of geometry, appearance, and language-aligned semantics from a variable number of views. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/f76be5fcde2e405bab5cdf18d7176f03/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The compact semantic-Gaussian representation addresses a practical limitation of pixel-aligned language fields. The ablations show that reducing embeddings from roughly 2.0M to 73.9K preserves mIoU while greatly reducing embedding storage.

The experimental evidence is broad: ScanNet and ScanNet++ results cover 2–32 input views, Replica evaluates cross-dataset generalization, and the supplement reports camera-pose and depth accuracy. Results are consistently strong across reconstruction and semantic metrics.

The component ablations are informative: instance-guided contrastive learning substantially improves semantic segmentation, while novel-view distillation improves rendering quality and mitigates the input-view degradation observed for AnySplat.
The paper is generally clear, well organized, and supported by useful qualitative comparisons and an explicit limitations discussion.
weaknesses: The method is an integration of a pretrained VGGT backbone, SAM2/CLIP pseudo-labels, voxel aggregation, and standard contrastive learning; both the coverage-based novel-view selection and DGLE are relatively simple. The originality is therefore moderate, and comparisons against alternative semantic compression approaches such as feature grids, clustering, or prior sparse language-Gaussian methods are missing.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the method's complexity. Important details such as embedding dimension, geometric voxel size, coverage threshold, contrastive temperature and sampling, CLIP/SAM2 variants, semantic-query decoding protocol, and several loss/implementation choices are not specified. The project-page field is also blank and no code-release statement is given.

The reported storage numbers count only embedding tensors: for example, 73.89K embeddings at the apparent 64-dimensional float32 representation exactly account for 18.04 MB. They omit the additional positions, scales, rotations, and opacities required by the separate semantic Gaussians. The savings remain substantial, but the paper should report complete semantic-representation and total-scene storage.

Efficiency is central to the motivation, yet no inference latency, peak GPU memory, rendering speed, or scaling curve with the number of views/Gaussians is reported. This is particularly important for an approximately 1B-parameter model and weakens claims concerning real-time or scalable deployment.

Evaluation details are insufficient in places. The number and identity of scenes in the Table 2 subset are omitted, no uncertainty or repeated-run analysis is reported, and the open-vocabulary class/prompt and thresholding protocol is unclear. LSM and Uni3R are also evaluated through target-dependent selection of two nearby views rather than genuinely processing the stated 4–32 inputs, so those rows do not constitute like-for-like arbitrary-view comparisons.

The evidence is restricted to indoor datasets; Replica changes appearance but not the scene domain. Consequently, claims about arbitrary multi-view images and broad practical applicability exceed the demonstrated generalization.

There are correctable consistency errors, notably the factor-of-ten disagreement between the semantic voxel sizes on the Figure 5 axis (default 0.16) and the accompanying text (default 0.016), as well as the malformed ScanNet SSIM entry “0.79.74” in Table 2. These do not overturn the scientific case but should be fixed.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: jointly reconstructing appearance, geometry, and open-vocabulary semantics from a variable number of unposed images in one feed-forward pass.

The decoupled semantic-Gaussian representation is practically motivated. The reported reduction from roughly 2.01M to 73.9K embeddings, with similar mIoU, suggests that dense per-Gaussian language features are unnecessarily redundant.

The evaluation covers ScanNet, ScanNet++, and an unseen Replica dataset, multiple input-view counts, novel-view synthesis, semantic segmentation, pose estimation, depth estimation, and several relevant ablations.

The novel-view distillation ablation shows a meaningful reconstruction improvement, while the contrastive-loss ablation indicates that instance-aware supervision materially improves semantic discrimination.
The supplementary material acknowledges important limitations, including dependence on VGGT, indoor-only training/generalization evidence, and difficulty scaling to hundreds of images.
weaknesses: The contribution is technically incremental for an Algorithms/General paper. Most of the system combines a VGGT backbone and heads, AnySplat-style voxelization, SAM2/CLIP pseudo-labels, standard Gaussian rendering, and instance-level contrastive learning. DGLE is primarily coarse voxel aggregation with isotropic moment matching; the manuscript does not clearly establish a sufficiently novel algorithmic principle beyond this integration.

The strongest comparisons are not convincingly fair. For 4–16-view experiments, LSM and Uni3R receive only the two views supported by their released checkpoints, whereas FLEG receives every available view. This demonstrates a capability difference but does not isolate model quality. The 32-view comparison with per-scene methods uses an unspecified validation subset, and no matched runtime, optimization-budget, or storage comparison is reported.

The semantic evaluation protocol is under-specified. The manuscript omits essential details such as the class vocabulary and prompt templates, treatment of background/unknown pixels, conversion of rendered embeddings to labels, mask filtering, and precise evaluation sample counts. Open-vocabulary metrics are highly sensitive to these choices, so the large reported gains are difficult to reproduce or audit.

The claimed efficiency and practical applicability are inadequately supported. The model has approximately one billion parameters and is trained on eight H200 GPUs, but the paper reports no inference latency, peak memory, throughput versus view count, or end-to-end comparison with optimization-based approaches. A feed-forward architecture alone does not substantiate the repeated real-time and scalable-deployment claims.

The storage analysis appears to count only 64-dimensional embedding tensors. Semantic Gaussians also store positions, scales, rotations, and opacities, while model memory and temporary rendering costs are omitted. Thus, the headline storage reduction does not represent total semantic-representation or system storage.

Reproducibility is poor despite the lengthy supplement. Important settings—including learning rate and schedule, optimizer, batch size, training iterations, geometric voxel size, coverage threshold, embedding dimension, sampling counts, CLIP/SAM2 variants, and several rendering/query details—are absent. There is also a factor-of-ten inconsistency: Figure 5 marks the default semantic voxel size as 0.16, whereas the accompanying text repeatedly states 0.016.

The evidence does not justify several broad claims. 'Any views' is tested only on 2–32 indoor views; cross-domain generalization is evaluated only on another indoor dataset; and the advertised 3D-editing capability appears only in a teaser without quantitative or systematic qualitative evaluation. Results also lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-run analysis.

Some quantitative reporting raises quality-control concerns. Table 2 contains the malformed value '0.79.74'; evaluation subsets are not identified; changing the number and likely distribution of target views across input-view settings complicates cross-setting interpretation; and selected qualitative examples with red callouts do not provide a failure-case analysis.

The method inherits geometric errors and semantic biases from VGGT, SAM2, and CLIP, yet robustness to pseudo-label failures, occlusion, inconsistent cross-view instances, uncommon categories, or out-of-distribution geometry is not evaluated. These are central risks for the claimed embodied and real-world applications.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: fast, pose-free reconstruction of language-embedded 3D Gaussians from a variable number of views. Supporting 2–32 uncalibrated inputs in one feed-forward model is practically meaningful and advances beyond methods restricted to fixed two-view inputs.

The decoupled semantic-Gaussian representation is a compelling contribution. The reported reduction from roughly 1.6–2.0M embeddings to 73.9K, and from 397–491 MB to 18 MB, preserves essentially comparable mIoU/mAcc. The sparsity sweep and dense-embedding ablations provide direct evidence for the central claim.

Results are consistently strong across ScanNet and ScanNet++ for reconstruction and open-vocabulary segmentation, including the important two-view setting where comparisons are least affected by differing view-count support. Supplementary experiments on unseen Replica data also provide useful evidence of cross-dataset generalization.

The ablations support the main design decisions: removing instance-guided contrastive learning substantially reduces semantic accuracy, while removing novel-view distillation degrades reconstruction metrics. Additional pose and depth evaluations further support the claimed multi-view consistency benefit.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with an intuitive overview and extensive quantitative and qualitative evidence. Overall, this is a convincing Algorithms/General contribution despite several evaluation and reproducibility reservations. weaknesses: The many-view comparisons with LSM and Uni3R are not fully apples-to-apples: these baselines receive only the two views nearest to each target while FLEG receives all available views. This supports FLEG's flexibility, but it does not cleanly establish superiority at exploiting the same multi-view evidence. Retrained or otherwise adapted variable-view baselines would make the case stronger.

The efficiency claims are demonstrated mainly through embedding count and float32 storage. The paper does not report end-to-end inference latency, peak memory, semantic rendering/query speed, total asset size, or scaling curves with the number of views. These omissions matter for a 1B-parameter model framed as suitable for real-time and scalable deployment.

Evaluation remains almost entirely within indoor-scene distributions. Replica is unseen but still indoor, so generalization to outdoor, object-centric, or substantially different capture conditions is unknown. Semantic evaluation is also limited to category-query segmentation; the advertised 3D editing capability is shown only illustratively and receives no quantitative or user evaluation.

Several details needed for reproducibility are missing or unclear, including the geometric voxel size, coverage threshold, embedding dimensionality, CLIP/SAM2 variants, sampling details, runtime, and exact query/evaluation protocol. The semantic voxel-size discussion also appears numerically inconsistent: the plot uses values such as 0.16 and 0.40, whereas the text states 0.016 and 0.040.

The method relies heavily on a pretrained VGGT backbone and teacher supervision, SAM2 masks, and CLIP features, so the algorithmic novelty is primarily in their integration, novel-view distillation, and semantic compaction rather than a wholly new reconstruction foundation. In addition, the 32-view comparison uses an unspecified validation subset for expensive per-scene baselines, and Table 2 contains at least one apparent numerical typo, reducing confidence in that particular comparison.
